query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification—specifically, the addition of a small fraction (≈5 at.%) of aluminum to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy—will improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, slow‐growing, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale without significantly degrading the alloy’s useful room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced by cast processing that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification via the addition of approximately 5 atomic percent Al (partially substituting or as an additive in the existing composition) to form HfNbTaTiZrAlx.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1000 °C) for extended exposures (from 5 h up to 100–200 h) while maintaining mechanical loading conditions similar to those used in previous tensile tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, adherent Al2O3 scale at the alloy’s surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Because Al has a very negative free energy of formation for Al2O3, its preferential oxidation at the high-temperature surface is expected to produce a continuous, protective alumina layer that limits oxygen ingress. This scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen and metal cations, thus suppressing pesting and catastrophic oxidation while leaving the bulk microstructure (and its associated mechanical performance) largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced weight gain and spallation during high-temperature oxidation compared to the untreated equiatomic alloy, while preserving its favorable room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which has acceptable mechanical performance but inadequate oxygen resistance for prolonged high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be effective under high-temperature oxidation conditions (approximately 800–1100 °C in air and exposures from 5 h to 200 h) and with only a modest (≈5 at.%) Al addition; larger amounts of Al or different operating conditions might alter mechanical properties adversely or lead to undesired phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum Al concentration and its effect on both oxidation kinetics and the retention of mechanical properties require experimental verification; potential trade-offs in ductility or phase stability, if any, are not fully quantified by current evidence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: (a) the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and (b) a modified alloy with approximately 5 at.% Al addition (maintaining overall near-equiatomic ratios). Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation tests in static air at 1000 °C for extended durations (e.g., 100 h) and subsequently perform mechanical tests (room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength) on oxidized and unoxidized samples.
measurements: Measure mass gain per unit area to assess oxidation kinetics (parabolic or linear rate constants).
Examine oxide scale morphology and adhesion via SEM/EDS.
Assess phase composition by XRD to confirm formation of continuous Al2O3 layers.
Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and yield tests at 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (lower weight gain and reduced scale spallation) compared to the baseline while maintaining comparable mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.

In summary, isothermal oxidation at 1000 and 1100 °C was performed on a novel RHEA for up to 200 hours, such long-term oxidation test has not been reported before for this class of alloys. The weight gain behaviours during the tests could be affected by evolutions of external oxidation, internal oxidation, and nitridation. The multiple stages of weight gain behaviour at 1100 °C were never discussed in previous studies since most of them only presented the results of oxidation up to 48 hours,. We believe that CrTaO4-based protection layer and Si addition may be important for future development of RHEA against oxidation and nitridation. However, it is also possible that the growth of a protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer was hindered by prominent CrTaO4-based oxide presence. In both cases, the nature of such CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in the future studies of RHEAs.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air.
